newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Employers, unions revive talks on plant closures.
newsitem.headline: Employers, unions revive talks on plant closures.

text.p: Representatives of European employer and trade union groups are due on Thursday to try and revive stalled talks on guidelines for consulting workers when companies decide to shut down operations.
The key issue is how to interpret European Union legislation on collective redundancies, which says management must consult workers in good time before taking a decision on their future.

The two sides began talks in April, at the instigation of the Dutch EU Presidency, in the wake of the much-criticised decision by French carmaker Renault to close its profitable Vilvoorde plant in Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
The European employers group UNICE and the European Trade Union Confederation ETUC have both openly condemned Renault's behaviour, which has since been ruled illegal by French and Belgian courts.
But they have been unable to agree whether existing legislation needs strengthening.
"It must be clear what 'consultation' means," ETUC spokesman Wim Bergans told Reuters.

"Consultation of workers meant in (Renault chairman) Louis Schweitzer's mind taking the train to Brussels, telling the workers at Vilvoorde 'We are closing' and taking the next train back to Paris," Bergans said.

He said ETUC wanted a clear, legally binding agreement with employers that the directive meant telling workers well in advance the company had a problem and involving them in talks on how to solve it -- where possible without redundancies.

The unions also want to bring forward the planned end-1999 review of the EU's works council directive, which obliges multinational firms with over 1,000 employees to "inform and consult" staff about major company decisions.
But UNICE spokesman Alistair Macintyre-Currie said the employers' group thought there was no need to tamper with existing legislation.
"The directives in place are strict enough," he told Reuters.
If the two sides decide on Thursday to abandon attempts to reach a deal, the unions will ask the European Commission to impose a clearer definition through new legislation, ETUC's Bergans said.
But a spokeswoman for Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said the chances of the Commission taking this up were slim.

The Belgian and French court rulings on Renault showed the existing laws were effective, spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told Reuters, adding that the union-management talks were never intended to produce a binding deal.

Nolan said a draft new EU law obliging small, national firms to set up works councils could help plug any gaps in the existing laws -- such as the absence of sufficiently tough sanctions on companies that infringe them.
A Commission official told Reuters the EU executive's hands- off approach was inspired by its reluctance to propose new legislation which the bloc's governments were likely to reject.
